Tech Scan: Sandbox

What untrusted code written by an agent runs in — and what stops it reaching the host, the network or your credentials.

This page is a draft. It covers the AWS-first sandbox default, the self-hosted alternatives that layer around it, and what not to build on. Entries are research references from web sources reviewed 11–12 November 2026, not locally deployed or benchmarked options.

Read the harness section of Concepts first: the sandbox is the runtime under the harness, not a replacement for it. The gates a sandboxed change must still pass before release are in Path to production.

On this page
Purpose AWS-first default Conditional alternatives Research-only notes Do not use Gaps and open questions Sources

Purpose

A sandbox is OS-enforced isolation for code an agent writes and runs. Use this test: if the agent's code escapes its container, the escape must land in a throwaway guest kernel, never the host kernel. A container on a shared kernel cannot pass that test — containers are not a sandbox.

Isolation alone is not enough. The sandbox must hold six trust rules:

  • Separate trust domains
  • Minimal execution roles
  • Explicit outbound enforcement
  • Approved dependencies
  • Protected credentials
  • Authenticated session ownership

A sandbox that lets agent code reach the package registry without an allowlist, or read the credentials of the session that launched it, has failed even if no container ever escapes.

Start from the managed harness with Code Interpreter for coding work. Add the Browser tool only for a specific task; do not add it merely because it exists. Gateway policy governs traffic through the Gateway, not arbitrary shell networking. Attaching a VPC alone is not evidence of package-only egress — network access limited to approved package registries — or secret denial. The egress and credential rules on this page are settings you add yourself, not defaults you inherit.

This page does not choose the agent, the model or the delivery pipeline. It answers one question only: what the agent's code runs in, and what stops that code reaching further than it should.

AWS-first default

The default is AWS Nitro Sandboxes, announced 9 November 2026: a hardware-isolated lightweight virtual machine per EKS pod, ECS task or EC2 workload, managed by the Nitro Hypervisor, at no extra charge beyond the instance, in all commercial regions, explicitly positioned for LLM-generated code and AI agents.[1][2] On EKS and ECS the sandbox is a Firecracker microVM running on Nitro instead of KVM, so each pod gets its own operating system and kernel.

Opting in takes one field on EKS: runtimeClassName: isolated-sandbox or confidential-sandbox. The runtime classes ship with every EKS Auto Mode cluster; standard EKS needs a sandbox-enabled node AMI (Amazon Machine Image). On ECS the equivalent is trustedExecutionConfiguration on Managed Instances only. On EC2, launch with --enclave-options Enabled=true, then run Firecracker from your own orchestrator or AMI.

There are two modes. Isolated protects the host and neighbour pods from the pod — the mode for agent-generated code, continuous integration and multi-tenant work. Confidential treats even the machine operator as untrusted:

  • Memory is moved out of the parent's reach.
  • Exec and stdin are denied.
  • Nitro Security Module (NSM) attestation covers the image and the Cedar policy.
  • KMS releases secrets only to a sandbox whose measurements match.

One caveat: without a KMS key policy verifying measurements, the measurement is recorded but never verified.

For networking, the annotation sandbox.amazonaws.com/network-isolated: "true" boots the virtual machine with loopback-only networking (no network access except to itself). A per-pod Cedar policy decides which images may load, which containers start, and whether exec, log streaming and mounts are allowed. Encrypted OCI layers are decrypted inside the sandbox with KMS, and AWS Signer-signed images are verifiable before they run. Pod Identity, VPC networking, EBS, EFS and S3 storage, and CloudWatch all keep working, and kubectl exec, logs and port-forward work identically in isolated mode.

AWS's own example runs a Claude Code agent via Bedrock inside one sandbox. The agent:

  1. Reads a GitHub issue.
  2. Reproduces it with a failing test.
  3. Fixes it.
  4. Runs the suite.
  5. Pushes a branch.
  6. Opens a pull request.

Egress is locked by an EKS ApplicationNetworkPolicy: CoreDNS and HTTPS to Bedrock and GitHub hostnames only. Model access runs through Pod Identity scoped to bedrock:InvokeModel*, and the agent holds one short-lived fine-grained GitHub token. A prompt-injection test that pipes a remote script into a shell never opens a connection, and when the pod exits the virtual machine is destroyed. A sample repository is listed in the sources.[3]

The limits, stated plainly:

  • Kubernetes 1.36 or later
  • No GPU passthrough
  • No snapshot, pause and resume with memory, live migration, or in-place resize
  • No published cold-start numbers, performance figures or service-level agreement (SLA)

Warm pools hide cold start — the Kubernetes Special Interest Group (SIG) agent-sandbox project claims around 2 seconds, validated by AWS.

The four AWS sandbox primitives — do not confuse them
PrimitiveIsolationRunsBest for
Nitro SandboxesPer-pod or per-task Firecracker microVM on your EC2Any containerised agent unchangedEKS shops; compliance or spend commitments; you own the cluster
Nitro EnclavesTiny locked-down VM, no networking, no storage, vsock onlyOne signed function: key custody, signing, PII tokenisationSecrets work — not a code-execution sandbox
Bedrock AgentCorePer-session Firecracker microVM, managedThe agent loop (Runtime, up to 8 h), agent-written code (Code Interpreter, fixed 2 vCPU / 8 GB), real web UIs (Browser, managed Chromium)Zero-infrastructure option
Lambda MicroVMsPer-session Firecracker microVM from a snapshot, own HTTPS endpoint; suspend and resume with memory and disk, up to 8 hA custom execution layer you build yourselfBuild-your-own sandbox API

Nitro Sandboxes were announced 9 November 2026.[5] Nitro Enclaves are GA since 2020, and there is no EKS-native enclave feature — the pattern is a pod on an enclave-enabled node driving nitro-cli. Bedrock AgentCore is GA since 13 October 2025, including in the Singapore region. Lambda MicroVMs were announced 22 June 2026 on the ARM64 architecture, in five regions without Singapore.[10][11][14] AWS added x86_64 support on 5 November 2026 and has since expanded regions, so check the current architectures and regions before recommending them.[15]

Runtime Instances is not per-session microVM compute: co-resident agents in an Instances session share a filesystem and can access each other's execution-role credentials. Do not treat it as an isolation boundary for untrusted code.[12]

AgentCore advisories

All five AgentCore CVEs from March to August 2026 were in the SDK and CLI toolchain around the sandbox, not a microVM escape — and the install_packages() one recurred after the first fix. CVE-2026-12530 (June 2026, fixed in 1.6.1) and CVE-2026-16796 with AWS Security Bulletin 2026-065 (July 2026, fixed in 1.18.1) work the same way: crafted package names lead to remote code execution inside the Code Interpreter sandbox, and from there to reading the attached execution role's credentials from the in-sandbox metadata service. This is package-argument injection inside the sandbox, not a host escape.[6][7]

Controls:

  • Pin bedrock-agentcore to 1.18.1 or later.
  • Never pass raw model output as package names.
  • Attach least-privilege execution roles — or none, since the default aws.codeinterpreter.v1 interpreter has no execution role and therefore no credentials to steal.
  • Watch for metadata-service access (169.254.169.254) from inside sandboxes.

Augmentation stack

Layer this around Nitro Sandboxes. The default, AWS-managed and least to operate: Nitro Sandboxes on EKS Auto Mode (isolated-sandbox; confidential-sandbox with KMS attestation where secrets are involved), plus AgentCore Code Interpreter in SANDBOX network mode — no internet, only internal AWS resources — for calculation, and Browser for browsing.

The controls below layer around Nitro Sandboxes. Each row names the AWS-managed control and the limit that decides whether it is enough.[8]

Augmentation stack — what to layer around Nitro Sandboxes
LayerControlLimit to respect
EgressVPC CNI ApplicationNetworkPolicy, a hostname-aware allowlist covering Bedrock, the Git host and registries, backed by Network Firewall and Route 53 DNS Firewall at the VPC edgeStandard NetworkPolicy cannot match hostnames; DNS Firewall stops the DNS channel, Network Firewall stops bare-IP egress; neither alone is enough
IdentityEKS Pod Identity per session, scoped to bedrock:InvokeModel* only, with IMDSv2 and a hop limit of 1No long-lived keys; a compromised pod cannot steal the node role
SecretsSecrets Manager and KMS, mounted with the Secrets Store CSI driver or the External Secrets OperatorNever stored in etcd (the cluster's configuration store)
AdmissionKyverno (YAML) or OPA Gatekeeper (Rego); Pod Security Standards Restricted; user namespaces (hostUsers: false, stable in Kubernetes 1.36)Map the machine-verifiable Instruction Manual 8 (IM8) and Agentic Risk & Capability Framework (ARC) controls to constraints; retain reviewed evidence and manual approval for the remainder
DetectionGuardDuty EKS Protection with Runtime Monitoring, plus Falco for eBPF detection or Tetragon for eBPF preventionFalco is detection; Tetragon is prevention
OrchestrationTemporal, or Step Functions with the AgentCore HarnessOrchestrates the outer workflow, not the sandbox itself

Conditional alternatives

Use a self-hosted sandbox platform only when you need a capability Nitro Sandboxes does not yet offer:

  • A sandbox API
  • Templates
  • Pause and resume

The platform gives you the API; the microVM still gives you the boundary, so run it inside Nitro Sandbox pods or Kata and gVisor RuntimeClasses, not instead of them.

Self-hosted sandbox platforms, run inside a microVM boundary
ProductWhat it doesStatusWhen to use it
E2BSelf-hosted sandbox API via TerraformGA; Apache-2.0; AWS support betaWhen you need a sandbox API and templates
Perplexity SPACESelf-hosted sandbox platform with an E2B-compatible API, per-sandbox egress gateway, and secrets kept out of guest kernels and injected at the network layerGA; Apache-2.0; v0.8.0, open-sourced 15 October 2026When you need a sandbox API with a reference AWS EKS deployment

Perplexity SPACE is young — version 0.8.0, with no production track record outside Perplexity — so treat it as a conditional alternative, not a default.[9][4] Standardise the lifecycle with the Kubernetes SIG agent-sandbox custom resources — Sandbox, SandboxTemplate, SandboxClaim and SandboxWarmPool, version 1.0 from August 2026 — whichever platform you choose.

Research-only notes

These are the primitives underneath a sandbox, for teams building their own sandbox. They are isolation building blocks, not a sandbox product: none of them on its own gives you:

  • A sandbox API
  • Templates
  • Lifecycle management
  • An egress policy
Isolation primitives, if you build direct
ProductWhat it doesStatusWhen to use it
Firecracker with firecracker-containerdMicroVM runtime and containerd integrationGA; Apache-2.0Building a microVM sandbox layer yourself
Kata ContainersContainer runtime with a VM boundary per podGA; Apache-2.0When a RuntimeClass boundary is needed without Nitro Sandboxes
gVisor (runsc)Userspace kernel intercepting syscallsGA; Apache-2.0; CNCF accepted September 2026Moderate-trust work; syscall-compat gaps remain
Bottlerocket OSAWS-managed host OS: SELinux enforcing, read-only root, no SSHGA; AWS-managed; mandatory in EKS Auto ModeAs the host OS under sandbox RuntimeClasses

EC2 nested virtualization is GA since February 2026, so Kata no longer needs *.metal bare-metal instances. That removes a cost barrier to the Kata route, but it does not make a direct build the recommendation — the default remains a managed sandbox with a self-hosted platform inside it.

Do not use

Do not build on these for untrusted agent code
ProductWhy notStatus
Plain Docker or runc aloneShared kernel — containers are not a sandboxGA; not an isolation boundary
Daytona OSSPublic repository archived and frozen at v0.190.0, relicensed AGPL-3.0; core development moved to a private codebase in June 2026; the community fork Nightona is still early-stage[13]Archived
SysboxLast release May 2025; does not install on containerd 2.x or Kubernetes 1.34 and later — treat as legacy; Kata is the replacementRetired
Runtime Instances for untrusted codeCo-resident agents share a filesystem and can access each other's execution-role credentialsGA; not a per-session boundary
Modal, Deno, Fly, Vercel or Cloudflare sandboxesNon-AWS sandboxes, out of scope under the AWS-only ruleGA; out of scope

Perplexity's September 2026 red-team report found network-policy bypasses in 7 of 9 platforms tested.[13] Treat that as a warning for the whole category: test the egress policy, do not assume it.

Gaps and open questions

At the time of writing, Nitro Sandboxes are three days old: no independent benchmarks, no published cold-start numbers, no service-level agreement (SLA) and no GPU path. Treat them as promising and verify in a pilot before relying on them. The warm-pool cold-start figure is the SIG project's own claim, validated by AWS — not an independent measurement.

Lambda MicroVMs Singapore availability is unresolved: five regions at launch, no Singapore, and a November 2026 builder article reports 14 regions without naming them. Check the current regions before recommending them for a Singapore workload.[15]

Next, read Path to production for the gates a sandboxed change must still pass — the sandbox bounds what agent code can do, it does not approve the change.
